data.name: Aniketh
data.gender_notes: Aniketh is used as a male name in Hindu naming traditions.
data.long_meaning: Aniketh is a Sanskrit name derived from the words ‘Ani’ meaning ‘without’ and ‘Keth’ meaning ‘desire’. This name is believed to represent someone who is free from worldly desires. The name Aniketh carries the meaning “Ani (without) + Keth (desire)” and is chosen by families in Hindu traditions for the positive qualities it expresses. Linguistically it belongs to the Sanskrit tradition and is also used in Hindi, Sanskrit, Marathi. Parents who choose Aniketh usually hope their child will grow to embody ani (without) + keth (desire) and live with faith, good character and purpose.
data.etymology: Aniketh belongs to the Sanskrit linguistic tradition and is used in Hindu naming. Its recorded meaning is “Ani (without) + Keth (desire).”
data.numerology_meaning: In Pythagorean numerology the letters of Aniketh total 5, giving a life-path number of 5. Number 5 is linked with Mercury and with the qualities of freedom, adaptability and curiosity.

vedic_reference.note: Aniketha is a name mentioned in the Vedas as a form of Lord Shiva, signifying his power over death.

historical_references.reference: Aniketha Chaturdashi is a significant day in the Hindu lunisolar calendar, especially in the region of Karnataka, India. It is the day when the ninth aspect of Lord Ganesha, Skandagauri, is invoked and worshipped.
historical_references.time_period: This day falls on the Chaturdashi (14th day) of the Krishna Paksha (dark fortnight) of the Hindu calendar month of Ashada (July–August).
historical_references.context: The worship of Skandagauri on Aniketha Chaturdashi is believed to bring prosperity, good health, and success in endeavors.

historical_references.reference: Aniketha is also the name of a 10th-century Jaina monk who wrote several commentaries on various Jaina texts. One of his most notable works is the commentary on the 'Prabandha-ratna-kosa' of Haribhadra Suri.
historical_references.context: Aniketha's commentaries have been valuable contributions to the study and understanding of Jaina philosophy and literature.
